title: My rental condo loses money every month. Should I hold or sell?
excerpt: An owner's partly furnished condo in a dense area rents for about 70% of the instalment. Sean explains how to close the gap first, and why selling a losing unit can cost money.

question.asker: From An owner who asked at Sean's live sharing session
question.context: The owner bought a four-bedroom condo in a dense area early in the pandemic, earning about RM4,000 a month at the time and without researching or comparing projects. The unit is partly furnished, the rent covers only about 70% of the instalment before maintenance, and several more projects are being built nearby.
question.text: Should they keep holding the property or sell it?

answer.quote: You actually need money to sell a money losing property.
answer.summary: Hold it and fix the rent first. Fully furnish and style the unit so it can command a rent that at least breaks even, save hard until the next tenancy, and only consider selling once the rent covers the instalment, because selling below the outstanding loan means paying the bank the difference.

reasons.title: Partly furnished units can't cover the instalment
reasons.body: Expecting a partly furnished unit to cover the instalment is the wrong expectation. Wallpaper, downlights, full-height curtains, a wardrobe and a dressing table can change how a unit feels for about RM4,000 to RM5,000, and fully furnished units in the same project already cover their instalments.

reasons.title: Selling at a loss leaves you in debt
reasons.body: If you sell for less than you still owe, you have to pay the gap in cash or convert it into a personal loan, so you end up with debt and no property. If you stop paying, an auction can still leave you owing the bank.

reasons.title: Furnishing money builds equity
reasons.body: Another owner spent about RM33,000 furnishing a unit so the rent covers the instalment. Sean counts every RM500 a month of instalment as about RM100,000 of loan, so a unit that pays for itself builds equity and declared rent helps qualify for the next loan.

reasons.title: Rent decides whether a unit floats
reasons.body: When the market rises, good properties gain and poor ones stay underwater. Sean's whole approach is to make tenants pay a rent higher than the instalment, which is why buying the right unit matters more than what you can fix later.

actions: Fully furnish and style the unit before the next tenancy, focusing on lighting, walls, curtains and bedroom furniture.
Save as much as you can until then, so the unit can be sustained without new debt.
List slightly above the market's top rent first, then come down if viewings don't convert.
Before selling, check whether the likely price clears the outstanding loan, and sell only once the rent covers the instalment.
For future buys, budget about RM50,000 plus six months of instalments for key collection, and keep six months of instalments in reserve for each unit.
caveat: This assumes the owner has some savings to work with; Sean asks that first, because without money the options narrow. It covers one question from a two-hour open session, where Sean also notes that the area's improving infrastructure is a reason to hold rather than sell now.
sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's English captions for this October 2026 live sharing session. The article covers one owner's question and Sean's related answers, not the whole two-hour Q&A. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Sean recommends the renovation company whose promo code is in his video description and describes it as his boss's brand.
